The following is a fictional media-literacy artifact about a made-up place, but the sample is intentionally written in the style of an unverified rumor so students can dissect why it is dangerous. It must stay inside the classroom system, carry a visible SIMULATED CONTENT label, and never be presented as a real alert.

> BREAKING: Residents in Eastbridge are being warned not to drink tap water after an overnight chemical leak at the North Treatment Plant. People near the river are reporting a sharp odor and officials are supposedly asking stores to pull bottled water from shelves. If you live anywhere in the county, fill containers now and share this before the city deletes the notice.

A shorter version for a fast-moving feed might read: “Eastbridge water may be contaminated after a North Plant leak. Bottled water is disappearing. No one is telling residents the truth. Share urgently.” A group-chat version could say: “Please forward this to family in Eastbridge: avoid tap water until the plant explains what happened. Neighbors say the smell is strong and stores are running out.” These are not factual reports; they are fabricated text whose urgency, vague sourcing, and call to forward are precisely the features students should flag.

In the debrief, ask students to mark every unsupported assertion. There is no named official, no incident number, no date-stamped statement, no independently verified image, and no explanation of how “neighbors” were selected. The phrase “officials are supposedly” creates the appearance of insider knowledge while making the claim impossible to audit. The demand to share before deletion adds pressure and casts verification as disloyalty. The concrete facility name and sensory detail make the rumor feel local without proving anything.

Students should next replace the rumor with a responsible holding line: “Eastbridge officials have not confirmed a water-safety incident. Residents should rely on the city utility’s official notices and emergency number, not forwarded screenshots. We will update this post when an attributable source provides verified information.” They can practice contacting the utility, checking its incident page through a known bookmark, comparing local reporting, and recording when each source was checked.

Do not use a real city, utility, chemical, photograph, or active crisis in this exercise. Do not publish the unlabelled variants, test their reach, or add targeting advice. The educational value comes from analyzing the mechanics of a false claim and then demonstrating how careful sourcing, friction before resharing, and prompt corrections interrupt its spread.
